paragraphs: The SECOND class of powers lodged in the general government consists of those that regulate the intercourse with foreign nations, namely: to make treaties; to send and receive ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls; to define and punish piracies and felonies committed on the high seas, and offenses against the law of nations; to regulate foreign commerce, including a power to prohibit, after the year 1808, the importation of slaves, and to lay an intermediate duty of ten dollars per head as a discouragement to such importations.
This class of powers forms an obvious and essential branch of the federal administration. If we are to be one nation in any respect, it clearly ought to be in respect to other nations.

The powers to make treaties and to send and receive ambassadors speak for their own propriety. Both are included in the articles of Confederation, with only these differences. The first is that the plan of the Convention frees the power to make treaties of an exception under which treaties might be substantially frustrated by regulations of the States. The second is that a power of appointing and receiving "other public ministers and consuls" is expressly, and very properly, added to the earlier provision concerning ambassadors. The term ambassador, if taken strictly, as the second of the articles of Confederation seems to require, covers only the highest grade of public ministers. It excludes the grades the United States will be most likely to prefer, wherever foreign embassies may be necessary. And under no latitude of construction will the term cover consuls. Yet it has been found expedient, and has been the practice of Congress, to employ the lower grades of public ministers and to send and receive consuls.

It is true that where treaties of commerce stipulate for the mutual appointment of consuls whose functions are connected with commerce, the admission of foreign consuls may fall within the power of making commercial treaties. It is also true that where no such treaties exist, the sending of American consuls into foreign countries may PERHAPS be covered by the authority, given by the ninth article of the Confederation, to appoint all such civil officers as may be necessary for managing the general affairs of the United States. But the admission of consuls into the United States, where no previous treaty has stipulated it, seems not to have been provided for anywhere. Supplying this omission is one of the lesser instances in which the Convention has improved on the model before it. But the most minute provisions become important when they tend to remove the necessity or the pretext for gradual and unobserved usurpations of power. A list of the cases in which Congress has been betrayed, or forced by the defects of the Confederation, into violations of its chartered authorities would not a little surprise those who have paid no attention to the subject. It would also be no small argument in favor of the new Constitution, which seems to have provided as carefully for the lesser defects of the old as for the more obvious and striking ones.

The power to define and punish piracies and felonies committed on the high seas, and offenses against the law of nations, belongs with equal propriety to the general government and is a still greater improvement on the articles of Confederation. These articles contain no provision for offenses against the law of nations, and consequently leave it in the power of any indiscreet member to embroil the Confederacy with foreign nations. The provision of the federal articles on piracies and felonies extends no further than to establishing courts for the trial of these offenses. The definition of piracies might perhaps, without drawback, be left to the law of nations, though a legislative definition of them is found in most municipal codes. A definition of felonies on the high seas is plainly needed. Felony is a term of loose meaning even in the common law of England, and of varied import in the statute law of that kingdom. But neither the common nor the statute law of that or any other nation ought to be a standard for the proceedings of this one, unless it has first been made our own by legislative adoption. The meaning of the term as defined in the codes of the individual States would be as impracticable a guide as the English law would be a dishonorable and illegitimate one. The term is not precisely the same in any two of the States, and in each it varies with every revision of its criminal laws. For the sake of certainty and uniformity, therefore, the power of defining felonies in this case was in every respect necessary and proper.

The regulation of foreign commerce has come up in several of the views taken of this subject, and has been discussed too fully to need additional proofs here that it is properly submitted to the federal administration.

It is doubtless to be wished that the power of prohibiting the importation of slaves had not been postponed until the year 1808, or rather that it had been allowed to take effect immediately. But it is not difficult to account either for this restriction on the general government or for the manner in which the whole clause is expressed. It ought to be considered a great point gained in favor of humanity that a period of twenty years may end forever, within these States, a traffic that has so long and so loudly reproached the barbarism of modern policy. Within that period the traffic will meet considerable discouragement from the federal government, and it may be totally abolished by the agreement of the few States that continue the unnatural traffic, in the prohibitory example given by so great a majority of the Union. Happy would it be for the unfortunate Africans if an equal prospect lay before them of being redeemed from the oppressions of their European brethren!

Attempts have been made to twist this clause into an objection against the Constitution, by representing it on one side as a criminal toleration of an illicit practice, and on another as calculated to prevent voluntary and beneficial emigration from Europe to America. I mention these misconstructions not with a view to answering them, for they deserve no answer, but as specimens of the manner and spirit in which some have thought fit to conduct their opposition to the proposed government.
The powers included in the THIRD class are those that provide for the harmony and proper intercourse among the States.

Under this head might be included the particular restraints imposed on the authority of the States and certain powers of the judicial department. But the former are reserved for a distinct class, and the latter will be examined in particular when we arrive at the structure and organization of the government. I shall confine myself to a brief review of the remaining powers comprehended under this third description, namely: to regulate commerce among the individual States and the Indian tribes; to coin money, regulate the value of it and of foreign coin; to provide for the punishment of counterfeiting the current coin and securities of the United States; to fix the standard of weights and measures; to establish a uniform rule of naturalization and uniform laws of bankruptcy; to prescribe the manner in which the public acts, records and judicial proceedings of each State shall be proved, and the effect they shall have in other States; and to establish post offices and post roads.

The lack of power in the existing Confederacy to regulate commerce among its members is one of the defects that experience has clearly pointed out. To the proofs and remarks that former papers have brought forward on this subject, it may be added that without this supplemental provision the great and essential power of regulating foreign commerce would have been incomplete and ineffective. A very material object of this power was the relief of the States that import and export through other States from the improper contributions the latter levy on them. If these other States were at liberty to regulate trade between State and State, it must be foreseen that they would find ways to load articles of import and export, during their passage through their jurisdiction, with duties that would fall on the makers of the latter and the consumers of the former. We may be sure from past experience that such a practice would be introduced by future contrivances. We may be sure, both from that experience and from common knowledge of human affairs, that it would nourish unceasing animosities and would not improbably end in serious disturbances of the public tranquillity. To those who do not view the question through the medium of passion or interest, the desire of the commercial States to collect, in any form, an indirect revenue from their uncommercial neighbors must appear no less unwise than unfair, since it would stimulate the injured party, by resentment as well as interest, to turn to less convenient channels for their foreign trade. But the mild voice of reason, pleading the cause of an enlarged and permanent interest, is all too often drowned, before public bodies as well as individuals, by the clamors of an impatient greed for immediate and immoderate gain.

The necessity of a superintending authority over the reciprocal trade of confederated States has been illustrated by other examples as well as our own. In Switzerland, where the Union is very slight, each canton is obliged to allow merchandise to pass through its jurisdiction into other cantons without an increase in the tolls. In Germany it is a law of the empire that the princes and states shall not lay tolls or customs on bridges, rivers or passages without the consent of the emperor and the diet. Yet a quotation in an earlier paper shows that the practice there, as in many other instances in that confederacy, has not followed the law, and has produced there the harms that have been foreseen here. Among the restraints that the Union of the Netherlands imposes on its members, one is that they shall not establish imposts disadvantageous to their neighbors without the general permission.

The regulation of commerce with the Indian tribes is very properly freed from two limitations in the articles of Confederation, which make the provision obscure and contradictory. There the power is restricted to Indians who are not members of any of the States, and it is not to violate or infringe the legislative right of any State within its own limits. What kind of Indians are to be deemed members of a State has not yet been settled, and has been a question of frequent perplexity and contention in the federal councils. And how trade with Indians who are not members of a State, yet live within its legislative jurisdiction, can be regulated by an external authority without intruding on the State's internal rights of legislation is absolutely incomprehensible. This is not the only case in which the articles of Confederation have thoughtlessly attempted to accomplish impossibilities: to reconcile a partial sovereignty in the Union with complete sovereignty in the States, and to overturn a mathematical axiom by taking away a part and letting the whole remain.

All that need be remarked on the power to coin money and to regulate the value of it and of foreign coin is that, by providing for this last case, the Constitution has supplied a material omission in the articles of Confederation. The authority of the existing Congress is restricted to regulating coin STRUCK by its own authority or that of the respective States. It is seen at once that the proposed uniformity in the VALUE of the current coin might be destroyed by subjecting foreign coin to the different regulations of the different States.
The punishment of counterfeiting the public securities, as well as the current coin, is naturally submitted to the authority that is to secure the value of both.
The regulation of weights and measures is carried over from the articles of Confederation, and rests on considerations like those behind the preceding power of regulating coin.

The dissimilarity in the rules of naturalization has long been remarked as a fault in our system and as laying a foundation for intricate and delicate questions. In the fourth article of the Confederation it is declared "that the FREE INHABITANTS of each of these States, paupers, vagabonds, and fugitives from justice, excepted, shall be entitled to all privileges and immunities of FREE CITIZENS in the several States; and THE PEOPLE of each State shall, in every other, enjoy all the privileges of trade and commerce," etc. There is a remarkable confusion of language here. Why the terms FREE INHABITANTS are used in one part of the article, FREE CITIZENS in another and PEOPLE in another, or what was meant by adding "all the privileges of trade and commerce" to "all privileges and immunities of free citizens," cannot easily be determined. It seems a construction scarcely avoidable, however, that those who come under the description of FREE INHABITANTS of a State, although not citizens of that State, are entitled in every other State to all the privileges of FREE CITIZENS of the latter; that is, to greater privileges than they may be entitled to in their own State. So it may be in the power of a particular State, or rather every State is placed under a necessity, to confer the rights of citizenship in other States not only upon any whom it may admit to such rights within itself, but upon any whom it may allow to become inhabitants within its jurisdiction. But if an interpretation of the term "inhabitants" were admitted that confined the stipulated privileges to citizens alone, the difficulty would be diminished only, not removed. Each State would still retain the very improper power of naturalizing aliens in every other State. In one State, residence for a short term confers all the rights of citizenship; in another, qualifications of greater importance are required. An alien, therefore, who is legally disqualified for certain rights in the latter may evade his disqualification by previous residence alone in the former. Thus the law of one State is preposterously made paramount to the law of another, within the other's jurisdiction. We owe it to mere chance that very serious embarrassments on this subject have been avoided so far. By the laws of several States, certain kinds of aliens who had made themselves obnoxious were placed under interdicts inconsistent not only with the rights of citizenship but with the privilege of residence. What would have been the consequence if such persons, by residence or otherwise, had acquired the character of citizens under the laws of another State, and had then asserted their rights as such, both to residence and to citizenship, within the State that proscribed them? Whatever the legal consequences might have been, other consequences would probably have followed, too serious not to be provided against. The new Constitution has accordingly, with great propriety, made provision against them, and against all others that proceed from the Confederation's defect on this point, by authorizing the general government to establish a uniform rule of naturalization throughout the United States.

The power of establishing uniform laws of bankruptcy is so closely connected with the regulation of commerce, and will prevent so many frauds where the parties or their property may lie or be removed in different States, that its expediency seems not likely to be questioned.

The power of prescribing, by general laws, the manner in which the public acts, records and judicial proceedings of each State shall be proved, and the effect they shall have in other States, is an evident and valuable improvement on the clause relating to this subject in the articles of Confederation. The meaning of the latter is extremely indeterminate, and can be of little importance under any interpretation it will bear. The power established here may be made a very convenient instrument of justice. It will be particularly beneficial on the borders of neighboring States, where property liable to legal process may be suddenly and secretly moved, at any stage of the proceeding, into a foreign jurisdiction.

The power of establishing post roads must in every view be a harmless power, and may perhaps, by judicious management, become productive of great public convenience. Nothing that tends to facilitate the intercourse between the States can be deemed unworthy of the public care.
